extracted.intended_audience: young authors and literary writers preparing periodicals, essays, and philosophical works
extracted.subtask_short: advice for young authors on publication
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and stylistic guidance for literary authors—especially those preparing periodical works or philosophical essays—covering language use (pedantry, neologisms), reading and interpreting mystical/philosophical texts, and practical publishing/business decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedantry consists in the use of words unsuitable to the time, place, and company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the scholar who uses technical terms in inappropriate settings and the man of the world who insists only on colloquial terms in a scientific disquisition may be pedants. Pedantry is judged by contextual suitability rather than mere technicality; examples contrast 'language of the market' used in schools and scholastic language used at the wine-table.

rubrics_metrics.name: When coining a new word is justified
rubrics_metrics.description: If you must convey a new sense, a new term may both aid recollection and prevent confusion with existing meanings (example: 'Esemplastic').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coining a term is not necessarily pedantry when the existing vocabulary cannot convey a novel idea without ambiguity. The new term should be made with awareness of audience and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer restoring obsolete-but-appropriate words to coining
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it is in our power to recall an unappropriate term that had become obsolete, it is doubtless a less evil to restore than to coin anew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restoring an old word avoids the burdensome task for readers of unlearning an old meaning and learning a reused meaning; coin only when restoration is not feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using old words with new meanings when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Using old words with new meanings demands a twofold exertion of thought—learn the new definition and unlearn the old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer introducing new terms (à la Linnaeus) to overloaded reuse (à la Darwin’s Zoonomia) because reuse increases reader cognitive load and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor vocabulary (technical vs colloquial) to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The language suitable for one company or occasion may be pedantic in another; precision must be balanced with the reader's capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-rate the acquirements of auditors; use technical vocabulary when the audience can follow, else favour clarity. The first lesson of philosophic discipline is to wean attention to abstract kinds—this may require technical terms, but only where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish and use technical distinctions carefully (e.g., objective/subjective, intuition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical distinctions (objective/subjective, intuition, sensuous/sensible) are necessary for brief and precise metaphysical discussion and may be reintroduced when convenient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such terms should be used cautiously and with authoritative precedent; they are indispensable for sound speculation in metaphysics, ethics, or theology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers of mystical/obscure texts must bring superior judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: To derive advantage or intelligible meaning from ignorant Mystics, the reader must bring with him a spirit and judgment superior to that of the writers themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mystical writings often require interpretive effort: do not expect plain exposition; successful reading demands active, discerning judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake simple, unlearned expression for pretence
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'It was delivered unto me', 'the word was in my heart as a burning fire', frequently mistaken for pretences to immediate inspiration, often reflect simplicity of soul rather than fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dismissing such writers as mere charlatans because of rustic or emotional phrasing; consider sincerity and inward feeling as part of assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious interpreting physiological/excited states as genuine inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Under strong excitement the man’s body may sympathize and he may mistake tumultuous sensations of nerves or fancy-spectres as parts or symbols of opening truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mystical claims with awareness that intense affective states can produce delusive perceptions; distinguish psychological phenomena from verified insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical truth sometimes requires symbolic or equivocal expression
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea in the highest sense cannot be conveyed but by a symbol; philosophers constrained from giving full answers for fear of personal danger or of exciting malignant passions may express themselves mythically or equivocally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that enigmatic or symbolic prose may be deliberate protective strategy; veracity is judged by intention to communicate truth, not literal exhaustiveness of statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: On attribution and coincidence of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity of thought or similarity of phrase is not certain proof of borrowing; coincidence can occur from common intellectual background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where resemblance exists, attribute what is obviously from predecessors but avoid charges of plagiarism for general coincidences; include references when truthfully possible to forestall suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and accept a small audience for abstruse themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers of abstrusest themes and truths that require effort of thought should anticipate a scanty audience; complex truths cannot be communicated or received without mental labour and attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be surprised or discouraged by limited readership for deep work; accept that market tastes favour easier fare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on subscription lists as proof of sustainable support
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscription names may be unreliable — they can be extorted, offered in jest, or signed without intention to pay; many subscribers drop out soon after initial numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat subscriber counts with caution when planning finances; verify commitment and be prepared for high attrition (example: many who subscribed dropped the publication before the fourth number).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid combining the roles of author and publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to unite the functions of author and publisher exposes the writer to insult, degrading anxieties, and financial risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most prudent mode is to sell the copyright (at least for one or more editions) for the best trade offer; prefer to let the trade handle sale, distribution, and warehousing even if their cut seems large—fifty pounds and ease of mind are often preferable to a risky greater sum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of trade realities and hidden costs (printing, warehousing, postage, tax)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-publication entails upfront costs (paper, printing), delayed receipts (subscription money received much later), and additional hidden expenses (warehouse/cellarage, postage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh practical burdens carefully before self-publishing; the convenience of trade distribution and avoiding long delays often outweigh the desire to keep a larger share of gross receipts.
